title: What is known about 1RB0LF_1LC0LA_1RA0RD_---1RE_1LA1RC_0LB0RC
description: Proof status of the six-state BB(6) holdout 1RB0LF_1LC0LA_1RA0RD_---1RE_1LA1RC_0LB0RC.
intro: This six-state, two-symbol Turing machine was one of the holdouts left open by the bbchallenge project. It does not halt from blank tape: Lean proves it, with a symbolic checker that the kernel proves sound, the round trips evaluated by the kernel and the long runs by compiled code (native_decide). This page lists what has been established about it, sorted by what each result rests on.
verdict: It never halts. Lean proves nonhalting: from blank tape the machine reaches one of 62 tape templates and moves from template to template forever. The 62 round trips are checked by the kernel; the start and the 62 ends of an epoch (2.5 million symbolic moves) by native_decide.

What it does. Each time B reaches the left end the tape reads B> 00 (01)a 000 (01)b 000 …, a list of counts separated by short words. The rightward sweep turns 010101 into 011001 and the leftward sweep turns it back. Each round trip takes 3 from a, while the end of the list runs through one of four periodic patterns (periods 15, 22, 16 and 9 round trips) and b gains 99, 141, 99 or 57 per period. When a is used up, b takes its place and a new, longer epoch begins: the first counts of successive epochs are 4, 12, 20, 38, 68, 122, 240, 484, 1002, 2104, 4375, ….

Why it cannot halt. Only D reading a 0 halts, after C>1 0. Every round trip of every pattern and every way an epoch can end has been checked as a symbolic run with the counts as variables, and each lands on a template again; a potential on the counts shows that an epoch always ends with the second count large enough for those runs.

claims.title: The halting configurations
claims.text: The machine stops exactly when it reads the symbol of a halting transition (D0); the generated statement covers every configuration.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10,000 steps
claims.text: The list simulator of the shared library, proved to agree with the machine's semantics, runs 10,000 steps from blank tape without a halt, evaluated by Lean's kernel.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps
claims.text: The same run, evaluated by compiled code.

claims.title: No halt in the first 10<sup>9</sup> steps
claims.text: The C simulator tools/c/triage.c runs 109 steps without a halt; at the end 39,660 cells have been visited and 19,822 of them hold a 1.

claims.title: Growth shape: sqrt/sqrt
claims.text: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.497). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.507).

claims.title: Shift rules
claims.text: B with a 1 behind it turns each 010101 into 011001 going right (14 steps a copy); C with 110 ahead turns each 011001 back into 010101 going left (22 steps a copy).

claims.title: The halting situations
claims.text: C>1 0 halts after one step, E>1 1 0 and F>1 1 0 after two, D>1 1 1 0 after three.

claims.title: A verified symbolic checker
claims.text: lean/SymCheck.lean: configurations whose tape is a list of cells and runs wn with n linear in some variables; auto finds the moves itself (a run crossed by a shift rule found on the spot, else one step) and compares normal forms at the left end. auto_reach proves that a successful check means the machine makes that run, for every value of the variables.

claims.title: The 62 round trips
claims.text: Each phase template B> 00 (01)3k+4 000 (01)3j+β rest at [k+1, j] reaches the next phase at [k, j + dj] (200 to 2,500 symbolic moves each), evaluated by the kernel. The tables also show that j + 2k + pot never decreases in a round and is at least 215 after an epoch.

claims.title: The 62 ends of an epoch
claims.text: Each template at [0, j+200] reaches a template again, with the old second count as the new first (4,200 to 127,000 symbolic moves each, 2.5 million in all), evaluated by compiled code; the kernel runs out of memory on runs this long.

claims.title: The start
claims.text: From blank tape the machine reaches template 31 (pattern R1, phase 16) with first count 118 and second 496, at step 1,277,431 (147,895 symbolic moves).

claims.title: It does not halt from blank tape
claims.text: The invariant “at a template with j + 2k + pot ≥ 215” holds at the start and is restored after a round or an end, each taking at least one step, so the run is defined for every length. #print axioms lists propext, Quot.sound and the two native_decide axioms.

claims.title: Four regimes, growing epochs
claims.text: How the templates were found: along the run, the list at the left end settles each epoch into one of four periodic patterns of period 15, 22, 16 or 9 round trips, in which the first count drops by 3 per trip and the second grows by 99, 141, 99 or 57 per period. Concrete simulations from every phase and residue return to a pattern.

claims.title: D never reads a 0 in 2·10<sup>8</sup> steps
claims.text: In the first 2·10<sup>8</sup> steps the machine is in state D 22,202,037 times, every time on a 1: the halting transition D0 is never close to firing in a way the run shows.

claims.title: Related holdouts
claims.text: The same table as 1RB0RD_1RC0LF_1LA0LB_---1RE_1LB1RA_0LC0RA up to renaming, started in another state; no common configuration in the first 10<sup>7</sup> steps of each.

explainer.lede: It never halts, and Lean proves it: the tape is a list of counts, the first one counts down by 3 on every trip, the rest of the list cycles through one of four patterns, and every way this can go has been checked symbolically. This page runs it in your browser and shows the counters.

sections.heading: From six states to one number
html: The question "does this machine halt?" is answered here by walking down a ladder of five descriptions of the same
run. Each level forgets detail that the level above keeps and has its own, longer unit of time. Each step down is a
Lean theorem saying that one move at the lower level is a real run of the machine, at least one step long, from one
configuration to the next. So a run that goes on forever at the bottom level is a run of the machine that goes on
forever: the machine never halts. The badge on each card says what Lean used to check that step
(Kernel: Lean's small trusted core; native_decide: a compiled
program whose answer Lean takes on trust).
A tape of cells and a head in one of six states. One unit of time is one step. It can halt only when D reads a 0.
Level 2A list of numbers
The tape as cells and stretches (01)n. One unit is one move: a single step, or a whole stretch crossed at once.
Kernel every move is a real run: sweep_right, sweep_left, auto_reach
Level 362 templates (t, k, j)
The list at the left end is template t with first count 3k + 4 and second 3j + β. One unit is one round trip.
Kernel (t, k + 1, j) to (nxt t, k, j + dj): round_0 … round_61
k counts down to 0, then the second count takes the place of the first. One unit is one epoch end.
native_decide (t, 0, j + 200) to (endT t, j + endC1, endC2): ends_ok; the way in: start_ok
Level 5One number Φ
Φ = j + 2k + pot(t). It never drops in a round trip and is at least 215 after an epoch end, so the next epoch end always has j ≥ 200.
Pick a moment of the run: the n-th time, counted from step 1,277,431, that the tape is one of the 62 templates.
The browser runs the real machine from blank tape to that moment, cell by cell, and reads its tape. It also runs
the shift-rule simulator of level 2 from blank tape, and the tables of the proof (levels 3 to 5) from the first
template. The rows show the same instant at each level, and the check marks say that the computations agree.

sections.heading: Crossing a stretch in one move
html: Between left-end moments the head sweeps across the long stretches. A stretch of a million cells would take a
million steps to simulate, but what happens to it is simple, and Lean proves it once for every length:
• Going right (sweep_right): B, with a 1 just behind it, turns each block 010101
into 011001 and comes out the other side, again in state B, after exactly 14 steps per block.
• Going left (sweep_left): C, with 110 ahead of it, turns each 011001
Each is proved by running one block for real (rfl, so Lean's kernel computes the 14 or 22 steps) and
then a general lemma, cross_r or cross_l, that says: if one copy takes the head through in
the same state, n copies do too, in n times the steps. Kernel
Any number of blocks. Type a number of blocks n. The browser runs the plain machine on the
rule's starting tape until the head comes out the far side in the starting state, and compares the step count and
the tape with what the theorem says.

Level 2: the tape as a list, moved by moves
A round trip from a template is a claim about infinitely many tapes, one for each size. Lean cannot simulate them
one by one. Instead it runs the machine symbolically: the tape is a list of tokens, single cells and
stretches (01)n whose count n is a formula such as 3k + 7. The checker steps
the machine on cells it can see. When the head meets a stretch, it tries one copy on its own (as in the panel
above) and, if the head comes out the far side in the same state, crosses the whole stretch in one move. If it
would need to know whether a count is 0 or not, it gives up and the check fails.
The checker is a program, auto in lean/SymCheck.lean, and it comes with a theorem,
auto_reach, proved once by the kernel: if auto answers true for a start and a target,
then for every value of the variables the real machine goes from the start to the target in at least one step.

sections.heading: One round trip, for any size
html: From one left-end moment to the next is a round trip: the head sweeps right to the far end of the tape and
back. What it does to the list depends on the short tail, which takes one of 62 shapes (the 62 templates,
named R0_0 … R3_8, see the next section). In each template the first two numbers are
a = 3k + 4    b = 3j + β   (β between 6 and 8, fixed per template)
Lean proves, for each template t and for every k and j: a round trip takes template t with numbers
(k + 1, j) to the next template nxt t with numbers (k, j + dj), where dj is a small constant listed for
each template. So a drops by 3 and b grows by 3·dj. These are the 62 theorems round_0 …
round_61, each a run of the symbolic checker of 200 to 2,500 moves, evaluated by the kernel.

the checker, so one run of the machine.

sections.heading: When the countdown runs out: from one epoch to the next
html: Round trips need k ≥ 1. When k reaches 0 (a = 4) the countdown cannot go on. What happens next has three parts,
and Lean checks them together as one end case per template. We call the stretch between two such events an
• The reset (three returns to the left end). The last 4 copies of 01 in a are used up and the
short word in front of b is rewritten. The old b ends up first in the list, with a few more copies. In the example
• The transient (up to about 145 round trips). Each trip still takes 3 from the new a, as before. But the
tail of the list is in disorder after the reset, so it does not yet follow any of the 62 templates. The new b
starts small and grows. Now and then two pieces of the tail merge.
• Settling. The tail falls into one of the four regimes, and the tape is a template again:
endT t, with a new k that is large and a new j that is small.
Lean proves, for each template t and every j: from template t with numbers (0, j + 200), the machine reaches the
template endT t with numbers (j + endC1, endC2). These are the 62 end cases, checked together as
ends_ok: runs of the symbolic checker of 4,200 to 127,000 moves each, 2.5 million in all, evaluated by
compiled code because the kernel runs out of memory on runs this long. native_decide
That is the step from level 3 to level 4: an epoch is k round trips followed by one end case, and at level 4 the
whole epoch is one move, from (t, k, j) to (endT t′, …) where t′ is the template reached at k = 0.
The first epoch end of the proof, in the real run. At step 1,908,405 the tape is template
R1_10 with k = 0 and j = 239 (a = 4, b = 724). The proof's end case for R1_10 says the run reaches R1_16 with
k = (239 − 200) + 81 = 120 and j = 259. Below, the browser runs the machine through it, from that step to step
4,054,968. The slider moves through every moment at which the head is back at the left end. The chart shows a
(blue) and b (green) at each of those moments.
<svg class="pw-chart" id="pw-ep1chart" viewBox="0 0 760 240" role="img" aria-label="a and b at each left-end moment during the first epoch end"></svg>

Why "j + 200". During the transient the new a, which comes from the old b, still loses 3 every round trip.
It must not run out before the tail has settled, or the end case would be a different computation. The symbolic
checker cannot ask whether a count is zero, so it needs a guarantee up front. The end cases are stated for an old b
of at least 3 · 200 + β copies (j ≥ 200). The longest transient takes under 150 round trips, so it uses fewer than
450 of those copies. The potential (level 5) shows that j is always at least 200 when an epoch ends.

sections.heading: It never halts
html: It never halts. Started on a blank tape, the machine
The Lean theorem is H36670.nonhalting : ¬ HaltsFromBlank in lean/Cert.lean, where
HaltsFromBlank is defined from the machine's transition table in lean/Machine.lean.
What it rests on. Lean's kernel checks everything except two evaluations:
start_ok (blank tape to the first template, about 148,000 symbolic moves) and ends_ok (the 62
end cases, 2.5 million moves), which are run as compiled code with native_decide because the kernel
runs out of memory (over 6 GB) on runs this long. #print axioms H36670.nonhalting lists
propext and Quot.sound, two standard axioms of Lean's logic, and the two
native_decide axioms, one for each of those evaluations. Nothing about the run is assumed: a wrong
number in the tables would only make a check answer false. native_decide
The proof is an invariant: a description of a set of tapes, called good, with three properties.
• The run reaches a good tape. From the blank tape, after 1,277,431 steps, the tape is good.
• A good tape always leads to another good tape. From any good tape the machine makes at least one step, without halting, and arrives at a good tape again.
• So the machine never halts. Repeating the second property forever gives runs of every length, and a machine that halts has runs of only bounded length.

What makes a tape "good" is levels 3 to 5 above: it is one of the 62 templates, a list of numbers written on the tape in a fixed pattern, with two of the numbers free (k and j) and the size condition Φ ≥ 215 on them. The second property then splits into finitely many checks, one per template and case.

Each round trip and end case becomes a computation: "does auto answer true on this input?". Who runs
that computation is the one place where the proof uses two levels of trust:
<dt>decide +kernel</dt><dd>Lean's kernel evaluates the program itself, step by step. This is the most trusted way, and it is used for the 62 round trips and the potential tables.</dd>

<dt>native_decide</dt><dd>Lean compiles the program to machine code and runs it. The kernel then accepts the answer as an axiom. Used for the start (about 148,000 symbolic moves) and the 62 end cases (2.5 million in all), because the kernel ran out of memory (over 6 GB) on runs that long.</dd>
Every piece, and what it rests on
Every piece of the proof, and what it rests on. A wrong number anywhere in the tables cannot make the proof pass: it would only make one of the checks answer false.
Machine.leanthe machine's table and what a step is (generated from the machine's name)Kernel
sweep_right, sweep_leftthe two shift rules, for any number of blocksKernel
auto_reachthe symbolic checker agrees with the real machineKernel
round_0 … round_61the 62 round trips, every k and jKernel
tables_okthe potential never lets j fall below 200 at an epoch endKernel
start_okblank tape reaches template R1_16 at (38, 163)native_decide
ends_okthe 62 epoch ends, every jnative_decide
nonhaltingglues the pieces together (the induction of the first picture)Kernel

#print axioms H36670.nonhalting lists propext and Quot.sound (two standard axioms of Lean's logic) and exactly two native_decide axioms, one for start_ok and one for ends_ok. Trusting them means trusting that Lean's compiler and runtime evaluated the checker correctly on those inputs. The checker's own logic is not trusted: auto_reach is a kernel proof.

Independent checks of the two native_decide pieces Computed. These are separate from Lean and do not replace a kernel proof, but they test the same claims by a different route, plain simulation with a small C program:

• The start: the plain simulation reaches exactly template R1_16 at (38, 163) at step 1,277,431. You can repeat it in the level 1 section; your browser does the same computation, and the one-moment panel at the top runs both the plain machine and the shift-rule simulator past it.

• The 62 end cases: each one was run concretely at j = 0 (b with exactly 3·200 + β copies) and at j = 13, and each reached exactly the predicted template and numbers, taking up to 2.6 million steps. The level 4 section repeats this in your browser, at j = 200 on the plain machine and at any j on the shift-rule simulator.

• The whole chain: the sequence of templates the tables predict was matched, in order, against the plain run from blank tape: 2,765 consecutive good tapes up to step 3·108, including 4 epoch ends. The one-moment panel at the top of the page repeats this match in your browser, one moment at a time.

A proof using only the kernel needs the long runs cut into pieces of a few thousand symbolic moves, with each intermediate tape written out (about 900 pieces). That work was started and is not finished.
The last lines of the proof, in words
<dt>Good c</dt><dd>c is template t with numbers k, j (t one of the 62), and j + 2k + pot(t) ≥ 215.</dd>

start_good
some run from the blank tape ends at a good tape (from start_ok).

<dt>good_step</dt><dd>from a good tape, at least one step leads to a good tape. If k ≥ 1 it uses that template's round trip, if k = 0 its end case, and the tables to show the new tape is good again.</dd>

nonhalting_of
by induction on N: for every N there is a run from blank of length at least N ending at a good tape. So runs of every length exist (not_halts_of_forall, forall_of_unbounded), and the machine does not halt.

sections.heading: The shape of the run
html: Left of the start, the visited part of the tape grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.497). Right of the start it grows like the square root of the step count, the signature of a head sweeping back and forth across the whole tape and adding a cell or a few at the end of each sweep (a bouncer-like shape) (fitted exponent 0.507).
After 109 steps the tape spans 39,660 cells (8,102 left of the start, 19,554 right), with a density of 1s of 0.5.
These are measurements of one bounded run, sorted by tools/py/bbtools/triage.py; the macro structure behind them is described above.

sections.heading: Related machines
html: Other holdouts of the list of 608 that are tied to this one. The comparison of tables is exact; everything about runs was checked on the first 107 steps of each machine and is an observation, not a proof (holdouts/related.py, holdouts/related.json).

Same table as the machine below, started in another state. Renaming the states as shown turns this machine's table into the other one, the halting transition included. The other machine starts in its own state A, which is not this machine's A: its run from blank tape is the run of this table started in another state.
